restatements.text: The measure makes possession of any amount of cannabis a misdemeanor, carrying a penalty of up to 90 days in jail.

analysis.answer: Current law allows adults 21 or older to possess up to one ounce of cannabis without penalty. The proposed measure eliminates this allowance, making possession of any amount of cannabis a misdemeanor punishable by up to 90 days in jail.

Direct costs include law enforcement resources to make arrests, laboratory testing, prosecution, public defender expenses, and the costs of housing inmates in jail for up to 90 days. Opportunity costs include lost wages or employment for those incarcerated and police time diverted from other crimes.

Taxpayers bear the financial costs of increased enforcement, court processing, and incarceration. Individuals who possess cannabis bear the costs of criminal penalties, potential jail time, and the collateral consequences of a misdemeanor record.

Cannabis users may hide their consumption, turn to illicit markets, or reduce their use to avoid arrest. Law enforcement agencies and courts will likely process more misdemeanor cases, which could increase local jail populations.

The measure addresses the perceived negative societal and public health impacts of cannabis use. The mechanism of criminalization and jail time reaches this by creating a legal deterrent, though it may create secondary problems such as increased burdens on the criminal justice system and the growth of illicit markets.
Police officers and prosecutors gain discretion in deciding whom to search, arrest, and charge for cannabis possession. Judges gain discretion in sentencing individuals to up to 90 days in jail.

The effect of criminalizing drug possession on consumption rates is disputed. Some researchers find that strict criminal penalties reduce drug use and associated public nuisances, while others find that criminalization has little impact on consumption but significantly increases incarceration costs and disproportionately impacts marginalized communities.
Substantial resources will be consumed in administration and enforcement, as processing misdemeanor drug arrests requires police time, evidence testing, court hearings, and jail administration.
This is a statutory change that can typically be undone by a subsequent legislative act or voter initiative.
